newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Group plans ASX listing bid for Australia woolpile.
newsitem.headline: Group plans ASX listing bid for Australia woolpile.

text.p: A private group is trying to buy Australia's 1.8 million bale wool stockpile for A$1.2 billion to form the basis of a company which would be listed on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) by about mid-year.
But the plan has run into opposition from Wool International (WI), the statutory authority which manages the stockpile selloff. The Australian government is non-committal.

David Sasson and Partners, headed by a former chief of the far east operations of U.S. oil major Amoco Corp, with County Natwest as financial adviser, plans to list its vehicle Australian Wool Trust (AWT) on the ASX if its overtures to buy
the stockpile are successful.
Sasson told Reuters it would be a A$600 million float.

The plan hinges on a proposed initial payout to Australian wool growers of A$1.60 for each A$1.00 of wool tax paid over the three years to June 30, 1996. This would cost about A$575 million and average about A$10,000 for each of Australia's 60,000 woolgrowers, Sasson said.
Half of the A$1.2 billion to buy the stockpile would be funded by bank debt, with the remaining half raised through the float to the ASX, he said.

Sasson said the plan would have to be approved by grower organisation Wool Council of Australia (WCA) and the Australian government to succeed. "We wouldn't have gotten this far unless we felt the government was behind us," he said.
He said his group was telling investors there was more upside than downside in wool, with production at a 20-year low and current wool prices producing negative grower cash flow.
AWT's acquisition price for the wool would be around present prices, but with a price escalator attached. Details of the price escalator remained to be negotiated, he said.
A survey of growers opinions on the proposal was currently being carried out, with results expected by next week, he said.
If the response was positive, a formal offer could be put to WI in the last week of May or first week of June, with settlements the last week of July or the first week of August.
AWT would be listed on the ASX if growers did not decide to take up 100 percent of its equity. Listing could be expected at the end of July or first week of August, he said.
Superannuation funds were seen as major investors in the stockpile, but could not presently be named, he said.
"The wool industry has not caught up with what the oil industry did 100 years ago and what cotton has done since...to have fully integrated companies," Sasson said.

AWT had signed heads of agreement with major Chinese and European topmakers with plant in Australia and planned to stay in wool marketing, processing, research and development when the stockpile was sold off, he said.
A WI spokesman told Reuters there was much concern about market confidence.
However, sources said WI expected net equity of A$700 million-A$900 million to be left for growers in its proposals to retire debt from the stockpile sale.
After paying off the stockpile debt of A$760 million, however, AWT would have only about A$440 million left, the source said.
A spokesman for Australia's Minister for Primary Industries John Anderson told Reuters it was a commercial decision for WI.
Anderson favoured proposals which stimulated industries but Sasson would have to work within guidelines, he said.
Wool Council of Australia said it had no policy on the matter as it was still a proposal.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
